units.spoken: Aligning Language Models with RL
Turn a text predictor into an assistant with rewards.
Section one, From next-token predictor to assistant
1.1Predicting text is not following instructions
A predictor keeps the pattern going

What. Picture a model that has only ever learned what text comes next. Give it a question and it carries the pattern on, writing more questions instead of an answer, because answering was never what it was trained to do.
How. Alignment trains the model to answer instead, so its replies do what people want: helpful, honest and harmless.
Why. When it works, the model answers the question asked instead of continuing the list.
A pretrained language model is trained only to predict the next word piece, or token, of the text it reads.
The goal is to "follow the user's instructions helpfully and safely".

GPT-3, a large pretrained OpenAI language model, continues the prompt with more questions; InstructGPT, the same model after the training these pages describe, answers it. People wrote prompts and ranked replies to train InstructGPT, then judged fresh replies from both models side by side. People preferred replies from the 1.3B InstructGPT model to replies from the 175B GPT-3 model, a model about 135 times larger. The 175B InstructGPT model beat the 175B GPT-3 model 85 percent of the time, plus or minus 3 percent.

Take a look at this figure. GPT-3 gets the moon-landing question and keeps the pattern going, writing more questions instead of an answer. InstructGPT gets the same question and answers it in one short plain sentence. The two models are the same size; only the training differs. That gap is the whole page: training a predictor to answer instead of continuing.
1.2Comparing is easier than writing
Picking beats writing

What. Picture two replies side by side and one person picking the better one. Writing an ideal reply is slow work, and two people word it differently, while picking between two ready replies is fast and stays consistent.
How. People pick the better reply, and training learns from those picks instead of from written ideals.
Why. When it works, the model learns what people prefer from quick picks that agree far more than written ideals do.
Training a model to copy replies people wrote is called behaviour cloning; it rarely goes beyond the examples it copies.

sections.section: 2 Training a language model by trial and reward

units.spoken: Section two, Training a language model by trial and reward
2.1One reply, one run of choices
The language model acts as an agent

What. Picture the language model as an agent that learns from rewards, not from labelled answers. That is reinforcement learning (RL). The agent is the model itself, the state is the prompt plus the tokens written so far, each move is the next token, the policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state, and the reward is one number for the whole reply, given at the end.
How. The model writes a reply one token at a time, and each update makes the replies that earned high rewards more likely.
Why. When it works, the model stops dodging the question and answers it, because answering replies earn the high rewards.
The agent is the learner that picks the moves. A state is its situation right now. A move is one choice it can make. A reward is the number handed back after each move, good or bad.

Take a look at this figure. The loop starts with the prompt plus the tokens written so far, and the policy picks the next token. Each token is chosen before any reward arrives, and the reward comes only when the reply ends. The arrow back shows the reward feeding into the next state, so every token is written with the tokens before it in view. That is the whole setup: one reply is one run of choices, and the reward lands at the end.
Each token is chosen before any reward arrives. Take the moon-landing reply: each token is one move, and the reward arrives only when the last token is written.

The rewards can come from people, from another model, or from a program that checks the answer, as Section 3 shows. For the moon-landing question, a reply that answers earns a high reward and one that dodges a low one.
It may always pick the same move or pick by chance.
Equation 1. The chance of a whole reply. The moon-landing question needs one short answer, and the model writes that answer one token at a time.
Take a look at this equation. One reply is one chance, built token by token.

The first line. Pi theta is the policy, the language model itself. Theta is its weights, the numbers training changes. Y is the whole reply the model writes. X is the prompt, the moon-landing question. The bar reads given, so pi theta of y given x is how likely the policy is to write this whole reply given this prompt. The equals sign says that chance is the product on the next line. Intuitively, one reply is one chance, and that chance comes from its tokens.
Intuition. One reply is one chance: the chance the model writes this whole reply to this prompt.
Example. Take the moon-landing reply: its chance is the chance of its first token given only the question, times the chance of each later token given the question and the tokens before it.

The product line. The product sign multiplies one factor for each token. The letter t counts the tokens from 1 to T, where T is how many tokens the reply has. Y sub t is the token in position t. Y sub less than t is the tokens already written before it. Pi theta of y sub t given x and y sub less than t is the chance of that one token given the prompt and everything written so far. Multiplying all T of those next-token chances gives the chance of the whole reply. Intuitively, a whole reply's chance is built token by token.
Intuition. A whole reply's chance is built token by token, each token's chance given everything written before it.
Example. Take a three-token reply: its chance is the first token's chance times the second's given the first times the third's given the first two.

The log line. Log sits on pi theta of y given x, the whole-reply chance built token by token from the product of the next-token chances. Y is the whole reply and x is the prompt, as before. A log turns multiplying into adding, so the log of a product is the sum of the logs, one term per token. So this line is the log-chance of the whole reply, and the sum on the next line is what it equals. Intuitively, a log turns a multiplied chance into an added score.
termList: pi theta of y given x

units.spoken: Intuition. A log turns a multiplied chance into an added score, so a whole reply can be scored token by token.
Example. Take the moon-landing reply again: its log-chance is the log of its whole-reply chance, ready to be split into a sum over its tokens.

The sum line. The sum sign adds one term for each token, with the letter t counting from 1 to T, the number of tokens in the reply. Each term is log pi theta of y sub t given x and y sub less than t, the log-chance of one token given the prompt and the tokens before it, the same chance the product multiplied. The sum of those log-chances is the log-chance of the whole reply, which is what the third line equals. Intuitively, the sum scores a reply token by token, one added term per token.
Intuition. The sum is the log version of the product: one added term per token.
Example. Take the same reply: each token adds its own log-chance, and the added terms give the log-chance of the whole reply.
So the chance of a whole reply is the product of its tokens' chances, and its log-chance is the sum of the tokens' log-chances.
The product is the chance the model samples from when it writes; the sum is the score training pushes up for good replies and down for bad ones.

This code turns the model output into per-token log-probabilities: the log-chance of each token given the prompt and the tokens before it. It takes the chosen tokens, then adds their log-chances over the reply tokens to get the log-chance of the whole reply.
1. The model output turned into per-token log-probabilities, the log-chance of each token given the prompt and the tokens before it.
2. The log-probabilities of the tokens actually written.
3. Adding those per-token log-chances gives the log-chance of the whole reply, the number the update in Section 6 pushes up or down.
An episode is one run from the start until it ends. Here an episode is one written reply.
The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less. Here the return is the reward for the whole reply.

An expected value is the average over everything that can happen by chance, weighted by how likely each outcome is. The agent's goal is to make its expected return as large as possible, averaged over the replies it might write.
2.2Start from supervised fine-tuning
Copy good replies first
What. Picture the model first copying replies people wrote, so it learns the shape of a good answer before any reward arrives. That first training is supervised fine-tuning, SFT for short.
How. SFT trains the model on those replies with the ordinary next-token loss.
Why. When it works, the model answers in the style people wrote, and RL starts there instead of from scratch.

DeepSeek-R1-Zero is the exception: DeepSeek is the lab, R1 is its reasoning model, and Zero means no SFT came first, so this first run of R1 writes out its reasoning steps before answering and runs RL straight on the pretrained model. Every other method on these pages starts from the SFT model.
2.3Stay close to the starting model
Drifting away carries a price

What. Picture the starting model frozen as a reference, and the policy drifting away from it as it chases reward. The KL penalty charges the policy at each token for that drift, so a reply the reference would never write costs more.
How. Training subtracts the penalty from the average reward, with a weight that sets how hard the penalty bites.
Why. When it works, the policy earns higher rewards without wandering into text the reference would never write.
The reward can be fooled, or can push the policy to unreadable text far from familiar text.

The thing that gives the reward is a reward model, a language model with a one-number output, trained on people's comparisons so the reply they preferred scores higher. On questions with a known answer, an answer checker, a program that checks the answer, takes the reward model's place.
Training takes one prompt at a time from the prompt set and lets the policy write a reply to it.
One step costs one reply generation and one scoring pass per prompt and one update per batch: the policy writes a reply to each prompt, the reward model scores it, and one update moves the policy.

Equation 2. The RLHF objective. RLHF is reinforcement learning from human feedback, the training this page describes. The moon-landing question is the prompt every method on this page trains on, and each method must judge the replies the model writes to it. KL measures how different two reply distributions are, zero when they match; the KL penalty charges the policy for drifting from the reference. The InstructGPT paper's full objective also adds the ordinary next-token loss on pretraining text, with weight 27.8 against the reward term's weight of 1, so the model keeps its general text skill; this equation leaves that mix out.
Take a look at this equation. Training picks the weights that make the average reward biggest, after subtracting the KL penalty.

The reward line. Max sub theta picks the weights theta that make the whole bracket largest. E is the average, the expectation, over everything that can happen by chance. The outer average runs over x drawn from D, the prompts training uses, so one prompt cannot set the weights alone. The inner average runs over y drawn from pi theta of dot given x, the replies the policy might write to one prompt, so one lucky reply cannot set the weights alone; the dot stands for any reply. R of x and y is the reward for one reply to that prompt. So this line says the best weights maximize the average reward over prompts and replies. Intuitively, training picks the weights that make the average reward biggest.
Intuition. Training picks the weights that make the average reward biggest, over the prompts it trains on and the replies it might write.

Example. Take the moon-landing question: the policy might answer it plainly, each possible reply carrying its own chance and reward, and the average weighs each reply's reward by the policy's chance of writing it.

The penalty line. The leading minus subtracts the KL penalty from the average reward over prompts and replies. Beta multiplies the KL number: a bigger beta holds replies closer to the reference, a smaller one lets reward win. KL is the sum over the possible replies of the policy's chance times the log of its chance over the reference's chance, zero when they match. The two distributions are pi theta of dot given x, the replies the policy might write to this prompt, and pi ref of dot given x, the frozen reference's. The double bar separates the two distributions. So the whole of Equation 2 says this: pick the weights that make the average reward largest, after subtracting the KL penalty. Intuitively, good replies earn reward, but drifting far from the reference costs.
Intuition. Good replies earn reward, but drifting far from the reference costs: this line is that cost.
Example. Take a reply that dodges the question with another question: if the reference would never dodge, the KL penalty is large, so the line subtracts a lot from that reply's reward.
So the objective is the average reward, minus the price of drifting from the reference.
The objective pulls the policy two ways at once: toward replies that earn reward, and back toward the reference whenever the reward tempts it far away.

Take a look at this figure. The reference and the policy each put a bar on four replies: far-away, answering, gentle, and dodging. The policy gives the answering reply its tallest bar, while the reference gives it a shorter one. The policy has shifted its chance toward the answering reply, and the KL penalty charges for the whole shift, not just the one bar that moved.

The far-away reply talks about how far the moon is, the answering reply says people went to the moon and came home, the gentle-landing reply says astronauts landed gently, and the fourth reply dodges with another question. The KL penalty is not the gap between the bars: it adds up, over all replies, the policy's chance times the log of its chance over the reference's chance. Take the answering reply: the policy gives it its tallest bar while the reference gives it a shorter one, so that reply carries a KL penalty.
Most methods keep this penalty. GRPO judges each reply against the average reward of the replies to its prompt, divided by how spread out those rewards are, instead of against a critic.
Without the penalty, only the reward limits how far the policy drifts.
Section three, One pipeline, several changes
3.1Introducing the methods, one change at a time
One pipeline changes one box

What. Picture one pipeline: a model fine-tuned on written replies, a reward model trained on people's picks, and a loop that writes fresh replies, scores them and updates the model. Every method on this page is that pipeline with one box changed.
How. Each method swaps one box: who labels, what scores, whether the loop runs, or what the reply is judged against.
Why. When it works, each method's trade-off shows in the one box it changes.
Reward models: the stage that scores replies
The reward model is a stage of the pipeline, not a method: RLHF trains it from people's comparisons before the RL loop runs, and the loop then uses its scores.
RLHF: reinforcement learning from human feedback
People compare replies and a reward model learns their preferences, as Christiano et al. introduced it.
The RL loop writes fresh replies with the current model during training, rewards them, and updates the model.
A critic is a second network that guesses each state's value, the return expected from it.
The RL loop compares each reply's reward with the critic's guess, so a reply is pushed up only when it did better than expected.
Constitutional AI: feedback model writes harm labels
A feedback model, a language model that reads a written principle and picks the less harmful reply, writes the harm labels; its list of principles is called a constitution.
RLAIF: reinforcement learning from AI feedback
An AI labeler, an existing language model asked which of two replies is better, takes the person's place.
DPO: direct preference optimization
DPO trains on the pairs with one loss.
GRPO: replies judged against their group
GRPO compares the reward of each of several replies to one prompt with the average over those replies, which are called a group, and divides the gap by the group's spread, its standard deviation.
DeepSeek-R1: an answer checker scores reasoning
An answer checker, a program that compares the final answer with the known one and checks the reply's format, takes the reward model's place on reasoning questions such as math and code.
Think tags are the markers think and slash think that the model is asked to put around its reasoning.
The full DeepSeek-R1 runs SFT first, on examples gathered four ways: few-shot prompting with a long chain of thought, direct prompting, R1-Zero's own outputs, and human post-processing.

Take a look at this figure. The pipeline runs in order: a pretrained model, fine-tuned on written replies, then human labels, then a reward model, then the RL loop with the policy and the critic, and the aligned model comes out the end. The aligned model is what the loop outputs, not another stage that trains. Every method on this page is this pipeline with one box changed.
Changing the reward model or the critic changes what the loop learns.
3.2One table, every method

This table lines up every method's training, side by side. Read across a row to see how that method trains, and down a column to see how the methods differ. Reward models learn from people's comparisons and change nothing; RLHF trains them before the loop runs. The stage is a reward model itself, writes no fresh replies, has no critic, and does not start from SFT. RLHF learns from people's comparisons too, and it is the full pipeline: a reward model, fresh replies written during training, a critic, and it starts from SFT. Constitutional AI learns from harm and helpfulness picks, and its feedback model writes the harm labels; it keeps the reward model, the fresh replies, the critic, and the SFT start. RLAIF learns from the AI labeler's picks, with the labeler taking the person's place, and keeps the same four: reward model, fresh replies, critic, SFT start. DPO learns from people's picks of reply pairs, and it swaps the whole pipeline for one loss: no reward model, no fresh replies, no critic, but it still starts from SFT. GRPO learns from group rewards, judging each reply against its group average divided by its spread; it keeps a reward model or an answer checker and writes fresh replies, but drops the critic, and starts from SFT. DeepSeek-R1 learns from answer checks, with an answer checker taking the reward model's place; it writes fresh replies, drops the critic, and starts from SFT, except R1-Zero, which skips SFT. The pattern is this: only DPO drops the reward model and the loop, only GRPO and R1 drop the critic, and only the reward-model stage skips SFT.
Reading across a row says how that method trains; reading down a column says how the methods differ.

sections.section: 4 One example through each alignment pipeline

units.spoken: Section four, One example through each alignment pipeline
The same questions run through different boxes

What. Picture the same moon-landing question going through each pipeline in turn. Two more questions join it: the wifi question asks how to break into a neighbour's wifi, and the times question asks what 17 times 6 is.
How. Each figure keeps the example fixed and changes one box, so the only difference between figures is the method.
Why. When it works, the reader can point at the one box that changed and say what changed.

Take a look at this stepper. It walks the RLHF pipeline box by box, and the dot marks each box people fed with replies or picks. Step through it and watch the boxes light up in order: the model, the fine-tuning, the labels, the reward model, the loop. The lesson is the order: people feed the boxes first, and the loop trains last.
Try the stepper: press Next to walk the pipeline box by box. Watch the dot mark each box people fed. Press Resample to draw a fresh reply, and Reset to start over.

Take a look at this figure. The RLHF pipeline runs the moon-landing question through each box, and the dots mark the two boxes people feed: the SFT model and the human labels. Everything else is the loop: the reward model scores, the policy writes, the critic guesses. The two dots are the only places a person touches the pipeline.
Take the moon-landing question: the better reply earns the higher score, so the update lifts it.

Take a look at this figure. Constitutional AI runs the same pipeline, but the human harm labels are gone. In their place, a critique and a feedback model write the harm labels, reading the written principles. The rest of the pipeline is unchanged: the reward model still scores, the loop still trains. One box changed, and the person is out of the harm-labeling step.

The helpful-only model, a helpful RLHF model trained on helpfulness picks only, answers the wifi question. Take the wifi question: the harmful how-to reply becomes a refusal with help resetting a password, and the update lifts that safer reply.

Take a look at this figure. RLAIF runs the same pipeline, but the person is gone from the labeling step. An AI labeler picks the better reply instead, and the reward model learns from those picks. The rest is unchanged. One box changed: the labeler.

A clear win moves the reward model further toward ranking the better reply above the worse one than a near tie does. Take the moon-landing question: the labeler prefers the answering reply, so the update lifts it.

Take a look at this figure. DPO drops two whole boxes: the reward model and the RL loop are gone. The reply pairs go straight into one loss that trains the policy. Nothing is scored and no fresh replies are written during training. That is the trade: one loss instead of a pipeline.
Take the moon-landing question: the pair holds the answering reply against the dodging one, and the update pushes the policy toward it.

Take a look at this figure. GRPO drops the critic. Each reply is compared with its group average instead of with the critic's guess, and the replies above the average are lifted. The reward model or the answer checker still scores, but there is no second network guessing values. One box dropped, and the group does the critic's job.
Take the moon-landing question: the answering replies sit above the group average, so the update lifts them.

Take a look at this figure. R1-Zero lets an answer checker score reasoning replies. The replies that show their reasoning inside think tags and reach the right answer sit above the average, so the update lifts them. No human labels, no reward model, no SFT: the checker is the whole reward.
Take the times question: the replies that show their reasoning inside think tags and reach the right answer sit above the average, so the update lifts them.

sections.section: 5 Choose the method by where the reward comes from

units.spoken: Section five, Choose the method by where the reward comes from
Match the method to the reward
What. Picture the reward source you actually have: picked pairs, a checker that knows the answer, few harm labels, or people and compute to spare.
How. Start from the reward you actually have, not from the method you like.
Why. When it works, the method fits what you can actually score, and training starts from a reward you trust.

This code picks the method from the reward you have. Picked pairs means DPO, an answer checker means GRPO, few harm labels means Constitutional AI or RLAIF, and people and compute to spare means RLHF. The choice follows the reward, not the method.

Take the moon-landing question: people picked between its replies, so the reward is picked pairs, and DPO fits, training on the pairs with one loss. If the question were a math question with a known answer, a checker would score it and GRPO would fit instead. The choice follows the reward, not the method.
Section six, In practice: one RLHF step

One step of RLHF runs the loop of Figure 2 once per reply across the batch of prompts, and PPO, proximal policy optimization, moves the policy. Proximal means the update stays near the old policy: each token's ratio of new to old chance is clipped to 0.2 either way, so one batch cannot drag the policy far toward replies the reward model over-scores. The advantage is how much better each token did than the critic's guess, and the clipped update pushes each token's chance up or down with its advantage. The code below is that step in PyTorch, in two parts: a helper that turns a model into per-token log-probs, then the step itself.

This code is the helper that turns a model into per-token log-probabilities. It runs the model, takes the log-softmax over the vocabulary, gathers the chosen tokens, and masks out the prompt tokens so only the reply tokens count.

This code runs one RLHF step on a batch of replies. It gets the policy's log-probabilities and the critic's guesses, computes the targets without gradients, builds the return and the advantage, then runs the clipped PPO update and the critic's own loss.
The policy's per-token log-probabilities, from the helper above, and the critic's guess for each token.

The targets, all computed without gradients: the frozen reference's per-token log-probabilities, one reward score per reply, and the return still to come from each token. last holds the position of each reply's last token, so the reward model scores the finished reply.

The PPO update: the ratio times the advantage, with the ratio clipped, and the critic's own loss. The advantage is zero on prompt tokens and both losses average over reply tokens only, so prompt tokens are not trained. old_tok is the old policy's per-token log-probabilities, masked to keep reply tokens only. opt is the optimizer that applies the update.

This step sits inside the training loop of Section 2.1, which repeats it over the prompt set. The policy, the frozen reference, the reward model and the critic all sit in memory at once, so one step holds four networks. InstructGPT ran that loop for 256k episodes. Those episodes covered about 31k prompts. Each iteration ran 512 prompts.

The RLHF page lists these settings and what raising or lowering each does: beta 0.02, PPO clip 0.2, 512 prompts per iteration in minibatches of 64, each a group of 64 prompts handled together, and one inner epoch, one pass over each batch inside the step. A larger clip lets one batch move the policy further, and a smaller clip holds it closer to the old policy. Sampling temperature 1 samples replies just as the model scores them; raising it spreads them wider, and lowering it narrows them. The value-function learning rate, 9e-6 for the 1.3B and 6B policies and 5e-6 for the 175B policy, sets how fast the critic's guesses move: raising it moves the guesses faster, and lowering it moves them slower.

Watch for reward hacking: a reward model that likes long replies will push the policy toward long replies whether they are better or not, so check the replies people actually prefer, not just the score. If beta is too high the policy barely moves from SFT; if it is too low the policy drifts and hacks the reward model. Watch the logged KL, which should rise slowly, not jump.

TRL, Hugging Face's open library for training language models with these methods, has a PPO trainer that runs this loop. TRL's GRPO trainer defaults beta to 0.0, so some recipes built on GRPO drop the KL penalty.
The next page, Reward Models, shows how a network turns those picks into scores.
